title: Does partisanship moderate the student-video effect?
rationale: In the source study, the student video 'Science in everyday life' raised trust by 0.063 (SE 0.025, p=0.012), and an exploratory arm-by-Republican interaction of 0.165 (SE 0.057) was found but never confirmed. All data came from Lucid, so we do not know whether the effect holds for Republicans or on another panel.
contribution: Provides a confirmatory, quota-sampled test of whether a short student science video raises trust more among Republicans, replicated across two panels.
limitations: Only one video is tested, so the result may not extend to other messages.
Trust is measured immediately after exposure, so durability is unknown.
Partisanship is self-reported, and panel differences may reflect other sample features.
Quota sampling on party may reduce representativeness of the overall population.

design.title: Partisanship as moderator of a student science video's effect on trust
design.overview: US adults from two panels (Lucid and a second panel), with about 50% Republican-leaning quotas, are randomised to watch a student-made everyday-science video or a control page. Trust in science is then measured with the source 6-item scale. The primary test is the arm by Republican identification interaction.
design.hypothesis: The video raises trust more among Republican-leaning respondents than among non-Republicans (positive interaction). Under the null (position b) the interaction and the main effect are near zero.
design.primaryOutcome: Trust in science: mean of the 6 post-treatment items, items 4-6 reverse-coded.
design.comparison: Arm (video vs control) by Republican identification interaction on post-treatment trust, controlling for pre-trust and panel; secondary: effect within each party group and each panel.
design.population: US adults aged 18+ from Lucid and a second online panel, quota-sampled to about 50% Republican-leaning.

assumptions: Power target: about 2500 per arm (about 5000 total) to detect an interaction of 0.1 at 80% power. The source exploratory interaction was 0.165 (SE 0.057), probably inflated, and interactions need about four times the main-effect sample.
Sample split about evenly between Lucid and a second panel, with about 50% Republican-leaning quota in each.
Republican identification is defined as Republican or leaning Republican, and registered as the primary moderator.
Pre-treatment trust is used as a covariate, as in the source study.
Panel is recorded from the platform; the panel question is a stand-in for that metadata.
unresolved: The student video file must be supplied by the research team.
The second panel provider, compensation and IRB number are to be decided by the research team.
The exact wording of the six trust items should be copied from the source instrument.
